question: What is @ControllerAdvice in Spring MVC?
title: @ControllerAdvice in Spring MVC — Global Exception Handling
direct_answer: **`@ControllerAdvice`** is a Spring annotation that makes an exception-handling class global — its `@ExceptionHandler` methods apply to all `@Controller` and `@RestController` classes in the application. It's the standard way to handle exceptions in a REST API with consistent error responses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Critical REST API knowledge — global exception handling is a must-know
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Handling exceptions in every controller method individually — not centralized, inconsistent responses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show complete @ControllerAdvice example with structured error DTO and correct HTTP status codes

sections.title: @ControllerAdvice Example
@ControllerAdvice Key Points
sections.content:
- **Global scope**: Applies to all controllers in the application automatically
- **`@RestControllerAdvice`** = `@ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody` — for REST APIs that return JSON errors
- **`@ExceptionHandler(ExceptionClass.class)`**: Maps exception type to handler method
- **Priority**: More specific exception types matched first; then general `Exception.class` as fallback
- **Error DTO**: Return a consistent error object (timestamp, status, message) — never raw stack traces
- **HTTP status**: Set with `@ResponseStatus` or `ResponseEntity` return from handler method
- **Validation errors**: Catch `MethodArgumentNotValidException` to extract field-level validation messages
- **`ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`**: Base class you can extend to handle standard Spring MVC exceptions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @ControllerAdvice is how you centralize exception handling in a Spring REST API. Without it, you'd have to catch exceptions in every controller method or use try-catch everywhere — messy and inconsistent. With @ControllerAdvice, you create one class and define @ExceptionHandler methods for each exception type you want to handle. These apply to every controller in your app. You'd typically use @RestControllerAdvice which is the REST-specific version. The best practice is to return a consistent error DTO with a status code, message, and timestamp — and never expose stack traces to the client. You'd handle specific exceptions like ResourceNotFoundException with 404, validation errors with 400, and have a catch-all for unexpected exceptions returning 500.

question: What is @ExceptionHandler in Spring MVC?
title: @ExceptionHandler in Spring MVC — Handling Specific Exceptions
direct_answer: **`@ExceptionHandler`** annotates a method that handles a specific exception type thrown from controllers. When that exception propagates out of a controller method, Spring calls the handler method instead of propagating the exception further.

interviewer_intent.testing: Exception handler mechanics — used in every production Spring app
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting @ExceptionHandler inside @RestController — only applies to that controller, not globally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ExceptionHandler inside a controller is local; inside @ControllerAdvice is global

sections.title: @ExceptionHandler Usage
@ExceptionHandler Details
sections.content:
- **Scope**: Inside `@Controller` → local to that controller; inside `@ControllerAdvice` → global
- **Multiple exceptions**: `@ExceptionHandler({UserNotFoundException.class, OrderNotFoundException.class})`
- **Method parameters**: Can receive the exception instance, `HttpServletRequest`, `WebRequest`, `Model`
- **Return types**: `ResponseEntity<T>`, `@ResponseBody`-annotated return, `ModelAndView`, `String` (view)
- **Exception hierarchy**: If `UserNotFoundException extends NotFoundException`, the more specific handler is preferred
- **Order**: Local controller handler overrides global advice handler for same exception
- **No catch needed**: Throw the exception from service layer; @ExceptionHandler catches it at the MVC layer
- **500 default**: Unhandled exceptions → Spring's default 500 Internal Server Error response

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @ExceptionHandler is a method annotation that tells Spring: when this exception type is thrown during request processing, call this method to handle it. You can put @ExceptionHandler methods directly inside a @RestController, but then they only apply to exceptions from that one controller. To make them global — applying to all controllers — you put them inside a @ControllerAdvice or @RestControllerAdvice class. The handler method receives the exception as a parameter and returns whatever response you want — typically a ResponseEntity with an error DTO and the right HTTP status code. The service layer just throws exceptions freely, and the exception handler at the MVC layer catches them cleanly without polluting your business logic.

question: How do you create a custom exception class in Spring Boot?
title: Custom Exception Classes in Spring Boot — ResourceNotFoundException Pattern
direct_answer: Create a class extending `RuntimeException` (unchecked) with a meaningful name. Throw it from the service layer when a resource isn't found or business rules are violated. Catch it in `@ControllerAdvice` and map it to the appropriate HTTP status code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Exception design pattern — every production Spring app needs this
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning null instead of throwing exceptions — forces null checks everywhere and unclear API contract
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the full flow: custom exception → thrown in service → caught in @ControllerAdvice → structured 404 response

sections.title: Custom Exception Pattern
Exception Design Principles
sections.content:
- **Extend `RuntimeException`**: Unchecked — no forced try-catch at every call site
- **Meaningful names**: `ResourceNotFoundException`, `DuplicateEmailException`, `InsufficientStockException`
- **Informative messages**: Include the resource type and ID: `"User with id 42 not found"`
- **Throw from service, handle in advice**: Keeps controller and service clean
- **Never return null**: Return `Optional<T>` or throw exception — both are better than null
- **Checked vs unchecked**: For resource-not-found, unchecked (RuntimeException) is standard in Spring
- **Never expose stack traces**: Handle in @ControllerAdvice and return user-friendly error message
- **Error DTO**: Consistent structure: `{status, message, timestamp, path}`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The standard pattern is to extend RuntimeException — that way you don't need to declare throws at every method signature. Give the exception a descriptive name like ResourceNotFoundException or DuplicateEmailException. The service layer throws these exceptions when something goes wrong — like user not found. The @ControllerAdvice catches them and converts to the right HTTP response: 404 for not found, 409 for conflict, 400 for business rule violations. This separation is clean: the service just throws semantically meaningful exceptions, the service doesn't know anything about HTTP, and the controller advice handles the HTTP layer concerns. You should never return null from service methods when something isn't found — it propagates nulls and causes NullPointerExceptions instead of clear error responses.

question: What is a good error response structure for a REST API?
title: REST API Error Response Structure — Best Practices
direct_answer: A good REST error response includes: **HTTP status code** (in body for convenience), **error message** (user-friendly, not stack trace), **timestamp**, **request path**, and optionally **field-level errors** for validation failures. Use a consistent DTO structure across all error types.

interviewer_intent.testing: API design thinking — consistent error responses are a production requirement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning different error structures for different exceptions — clients can't parse them reliably
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete ErrorResponse DTO and mention RFC 7807 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs)

sections.title: Error Response DTO
Error Response Best Practices
sections.content:
- **Consistent structure**: Every error from every endpoint returns the same JSON shape
- **HTTP status code**: Set in the HTTP response status AND include in the body for easy client parsing
- **User-friendly message**: Human-readable — no Java class names, no stack traces
- **Timestamp**: ISO-8601 format (`LocalDateTime` serialized properly)
- **Path**: The request URI that caused the error
- **Field errors**: For 400 validation errors, include which fields failed and why
- **NEVER include**: Full stack trace, internal package names, database error details
- **RFC 7807**: Problem Details for HTTP APIs — standard format with `type`, `title`, `detail`, `instance`
- **Spring Boot default**: `/error` endpoint returns basic error JSON — customize with @ControllerAdvice
- **No sensitive data**: Don't expose internal system info (DB table names, connection strings)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A good REST error response should be consistent — every error from your API should have the same JSON structure so clients can reliably parse it. The essential fields are: the HTTP status code repeated in the body for convenience, a clear human-readable error message, the timestamp, and the request path. For validation errors, include a list of field-specific errors so the client knows which fields were invalid and why. What you should absolutely NOT include is the Java stack trace, internal class names, or database error messages — these expose implementation details and are security risks. Consistency matters most: if your 404 response looks different from your 400 response, clients have to write different parsing logic for each error type.

question: What is ResponseEntityExceptionHandler in Spring MVC?
title: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler — Base Class for Spring MVC Exception Handling
direct_answer: **`ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`** is a base class your `@ControllerAdvice` can extend to get built-in handling for standard Spring MVC exceptions like `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, `NoHandlerFoundException`, `HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException`, and others — with proper HTTP status codes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Spring's built-in exception handling utilities
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing this class exists — reinventing handling for standard Spring exceptions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific Spring MVC exceptions it handles and how you override them

sections.title: Using ResponseEntityExceptionHandler
Exceptions Handled by Base Class
sections.content:
- **`MethodArgumentNotValidException`**: `@Valid` validation failure → 400
- **`NoHandlerFoundException`**: URL has no matching controller → 404
- **`HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException`**: Wrong HTTP method for URL → 405
- **`HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`**: Wrong Content-Type → 415
- **`HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException`**: Can't produce requested Accept type → 406
- **`MissingServletRequestParameterException`**: Required @RequestParam missing → 400
- **`BindException`**: Form binding failure → 400
- **Strategy**: Extend this base class → override the methods you want to customize → add @ExceptionHandler for your custom exceptions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler is a convenience base class provided by Spring MVC that your @ControllerAdvice can extend. It already has @ExceptionHandler methods for all the standard Spring MVC exceptions — things like validation failures, wrong HTTP method, missing request parameters, unsupported content types — and returns appropriate HTTP status codes for each. Instead of writing those handlers yourself, you extend this class and just override the ones you want to customize. Then you add your own @ExceptionHandler methods for your application-specific exceptions. It saves boilerplate and ensures you don't accidentally miss proper status codes for standard Spring exceptions. It's a good base class to know about for production-quality exception handling.

question: What are best practices for exception handling in a Spring REST API?
title: Exception Handling Best Practices in Spring REST API
direct_answer: Best practices: use **`@RestControllerAdvice`** for global handling, create **meaningful custom exceptions** per business case, return **consistent error DTOs** (never stack traces), use **correct HTTP status codes** (404 for not found, 400 for validation, 500 for server errors), and log exceptions server-side.

interviewer_intent.testing: Judgment and best practices — shows production experience
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Catching all exceptions with Exception.class only and returning generic 500 — no fine-grained error differentiation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Cover all five best practices: global advice, meaningful exceptions, consistent DTOs, correct codes, server-side logging

sections.title: Exception Handling Checklist
sections.content:
**5 best practices:**

1. **Centralize handling**: `@RestControllerAdvice` — one place for all error responses
2. **Meaningful exceptions**: `ResourceNotFoundException`, `DuplicateEmailException` — not generic `RuntimeException`
3. **Consistent error DTO**: Same JSON structure for every error
4. **Correct HTTP codes**: 400 (bad input), 401 (auth), 403 (forbidden), 404 (not found), 409 (conflict), 500 (server)
5. **Log server-side**: Log exceptions with `log.error()` — never expose stack traces to clients

sections.title: Best Practices Summary
sections.content:
- **@RestControllerAdvice**: Single global exception handler class
- **Service throws, advice catches**: No HTTP exception handling in service layer
- **Custom exceptions per domain**: `UserNotFoundException`, `InsufficientInventoryException` — meaningful
- **Never expose**: Stack traces, internal class names, DB error details in response body
- **Always log**: `log.error("Exception handling request", ex)` — essential for debugging production issues
- **Specific before general**: Handle `ResourceNotFoundException` before `Exception` — spring uses first match
- **Validation errors**: Return field-level errors list, not just 'validation failed'
- **Consistent format**: Same DTO structure across all error responses
- **Document errors**: Swagger/OpenAPI error schemas help API consumers
- **Test error paths**: Write tests for error scenarios as rigorously as success scenarios

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Good exception handling in a Spring REST API has a few key pillars. First, centralize everything in a @RestControllerAdvice class — don't scatter try-catch blocks through controllers. Second, create meaningful custom exceptions named after what went wrong business-wise, not generic RuntimeExceptions. Third, always return a consistent error DTO structure — timestamp, status, message, path — so clients can parse errors predictably. Fourth, use the right HTTP status codes — 404 for resources not found, 400 for validation failures, 409 for conflicts, 500 for unexpected errors. Fifth, always log the exception server-side with a proper log.error call — you need the stack trace for debugging, but it should never reach the client. Testing your error paths is just as important as testing success paths.
